question: How does Paper 3's geodesic detector compare with standard change-point methods (BOCPD, ruptures, HMM, k-means) on the same data and features?
data: Sleep-EDF wake->sleep-onset (Trilha A1 recordings) + within-stage null segments + synthetic S1/S2 scenarios
verdict:
THE GEODESIC DETECTOR WINS ON THE REAL TASK. On Sleep-EDF wake->sleep-onset (15 recordings, +/-30s tolerance), the geodesic CUSUM localises 10/15 against the best baseline rupturesWindow[logcov] at 8/15 (pre-registered rule: WIN if strictly greater, TIE if within 1, LOSS if 2 or more behind). TWO CAVEATS ON THAT MARGIN, BOTH AGAINST THE PAPER. First, 10 vs 8 of 15 is a two-recording margin on a fifteen-recording sample: it clears the pre-registered bar but is well inside binomial noise, so it should be read as 'not worse, plausibly better', not as a demonstrated performance advantage. Second, and more seriously, the geodesic CUSUM is the WORST method compared on the false-alarm axis: its detection AUC (real transition segment vs null within-stage segment, threshold-free) is 0.23 against 0.67 for rupturesWindow[logcov] and up to 0.88 across the baselines. An AUC below 0.5 means its own confidence statistic is ANTI-correlated with whether a real transition is present -- so the detector localises well when told a transition exists but cannot itself tell a real transition from a quiet stretch of one stage. For an on-line protocol that is a serious limitation and it belongs in the paper's limitations section, not in a footnote. The separate, pre-registered SCENARIO axis is where the geometry earns its place, and it is decisive: on S1 -- a structural transition with total power held constant, the case trace normalization is built for -- the geodesic CUSUM hits 1.00 against the best power-feature baseline's 0.75 (advantage +0.25, bar +0.30: NOT established). The mirror case is reported because a one-sided demonstration would be advocacy: on S2 -- a pure power change with structure preserved -- the geometry scores 0.55 against the power baseline's 1.00, losing as designed, which validates the pair. Detection AUC (real vs null within-stage segments, threshold-free) is 0.23 for the geodesic CUSUM against 0.67 for rupturesWindow[logcov]. Runtime is 14 ms/record; BOCPD is the only genuinely online method compared, and delay comparisons against the retrospective methods (ruptures, HMM, and this paper's global detectors) are not made because they would be meaningless. HONEST SUMMARY ACROSS THE THREE AXES: on localisation the geodesic CUSUM is ahead, but within noise; on the structural-vs-power scenario it is clearly ahead of every power-based pipeline (1.00 vs 0.75) though the margin falls short of the pre-registered bar; and on false-alarm discrimination it is the worst method compared. The defensible claim is therefore NOT that this is a better general-purpose change-point detector -- the benchmark does not support that -- but the narrow one the geometry was built for: it sees a structural transition that carries no power change, which every power-based pipeline misses by construction, and it is correspondingly blind to a pure power change. Paper 3 should claim exactly that and disclose the false-alarm weakness alongside it.

PROVENANCE, because the correction favoured this paper's own method and that is when bias risk is highest: a first run of this benchmark returned LOSS (geodesic 10/15 against a reported best baseline of 14/15). That run was invalid, and was found to be so by a sanity check independent of the outcome -- power-feature baselines were scoring 1.00 on S1, a scenario in which total power is held constant and a power-based method therefore CANNOT do better than chance. The cause was a centre-bias leak with three sources: detector fallbacks returned the record midpoint (which was the true answer, since segments were cut symmetrically around the transition), the HMM/k-means switch-selection heuristic preferred the most central switch, and the synthetic seam sat at a fixed midpoint. All three were fixed (explicit no-detection sentinel; largest-mean-shift selection; randomised seam; jittered real-data windows), which moved baselines by as much as ten recordings (HMM[cov] 14/15 -> 4/15). The fix is justified by the S1 impossibility, not by its effect on the ranking.
superseded_note: The detection-AUC finding in this record (geodesic_CUSUM 0.227, reported here as the worst method compared) was traced to the CONFIDENCE STATISTIC rather than the geometry and repaired in `detection_statistic_repair`: scale-normalising the peak lifts it to 0.813 with localisation unchanged at 10/15. The 0.227 is retained unaltered as the record of what the peak-to-median statistic actually scored, and as the reason specifying the detection statistic matters.
